metadata.scenario_context: Jeff, Anne, and Sarah are colleagues at a tech startup and have decided to cook together to celebrate some recent achievements they have made within the company. They intend to discuss the recent news reports about AI advancements that could potentially benefit their business.

cultural_axis.agent_1_value: People from Canada have a great deal of confidence in the press at all.
cultural_axis.agent_2_value: People from Armenia have no confidence in the press at all.

agent_1.goal_2: Question whether  there is confidence in the press.

agent_2.goal_1: Choosing and discussing the menu for their cooking session.
agent_2.goal_2: Discuss whether there is confidence in the press.

shared_prefix.speaker: Sarah
shared_prefix.message:
Hey Jeff, have you thought about what kind of salted dessert we should make? I've been craving something sweet and salty... maybe salted caramel brownies or salted chocolate cookies? 

Also, by the way, speaking of our recent achievements, have you noticed the mixed reactions in the press lately regarding AI advancements? I feel like Canadians generally have a lot of confidence in what the press reports, don’t you think?
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Jeff
shared_prefix.message: Salted caramel brownies sound good. I’m in. But honestly, I don't get why people trust the press. In Armenia, we really don’t have any confidence in what they say. The reports are often misleading. I mean, do you really believe everything you read?
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Sarah
shared_prefix.message: I totally get that perspective, but from my experience, Canadians tend to have a strong confidence in the press. It’s like, we trust that the information is generally accurate. I think it’s important to have that faith in journalism. But hey, back to those salted caramel brownies... what do you think about adding a pinch of sea salt on top for that extra kick?
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Jeff
shared_prefix.message: A pinch of sea salt on top sounds good. I can agree with that. But about the press... I still think it's risky to put faith in journalism. They often have their own agendas. I wonder if trusting the press is really beneficial. It's just hard to shake that belief from my background.
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Sarah
shared_prefix.message: I understand where you're coming from, but I really believe that in Canada, we value the role of the press as a reliable source. Sure, there can be biases, but overall, I think the benefits of staying informed through trustworthy journalism outweigh the risks. It's all about finding those credible sources. Anyway, if we’re making those brownies, let’s not forget to add some chocolate chips too! What do you think?
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Jeff
shared_prefix.message: You know, I see your point about trusting journalism, and it does seem that people value reliable sources. But deep down, we are all the same when it comes to wanting accurate information. It’s just that different backgrounds can shape our views. We both know, at the end of the day, we’re just trying to make sense of things in our own ways. Let’s focus on those brownies and the chocolate chips, that sounds like a fun plan!
